overview: Winton Land is a New Zealand-based property group that masterplans, develops and sells residential land and dwellings, and increasingly operates a diversified portfolio of retirement living, commercial and hospitality/leisure assets built on its landbank. Winton's core model is buying and rezoning large tracts of land, subdividing them into masterplanned communities (Northlake, Lakeside, Sunfield, Launch Bay and others across New Zealand and one project in Cessnock, Australia), and pre-selling sections/dwellings ahead of construction. It has been dual-listed on the NZX and ASX since its 2021 IPO and is majority-controlled (~55%) by founder Chris Meehan, with Macquarie Asset Management the second-largest holder (~22%).

business_model.summary: Winton generates the bulk of revenue from settling pre-sold residential land lots, townhouses and apartments across its masterplanned communities, recognized on unconditional settlement (a lumpy, project-milestone-driven revenue pattern rather than smooth recurring income). It is increasingly diversifying into recurring revenue: retirement village occupation right agreements (Northbrook Wānaka, which opened its first stage in May 2025), commercial office leasing (Cracker Bay, Auckland waterfront), and hospitality/leisure (Ayrburn precinct in Arrowtown - restaurants, event venues, and tourist attraction, its first full year of trading in FY25). A pre-sale book (contracted but unsettled sales, $239.8m as at 31 Dec 2025) underpins forward revenue visibility but is itself a lagging indicator of a slowing market.
business_model.customer_type: B2C - individual homebuyers, downsizers/retirees, and office tenants/hospitality visitors
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand-concentrated (Auckland/Sunfield, Hobsonville, Te Kauwhata/Lakeside, Wānaka/Northlake and Northbrook, Arrowtown/Ayrburn) with one Australian project (North Ridge, Cessnock, NSW); dual-listed NZX/ASX

main_competitors: Kāinga Ora (state housing developer, also a litigant/counterparty)
competitive_position.market_position: Niche but sizeable developer of large-scale masterplanned communities with a ~5,750-unit landbank pipeline; a relatively small-cap ($300-400m market cap range) compared to diversified peers, with concentrated exposure to a handful of large projects

moat_factors.description: c.5,750 unit pipeline across 20 projects with consenting/planning work largely done, a multi-year runway that is costly and slow for new entrants to replicate
Selling sections ahead of construction reduces speculative build risk and partially locks in revenue, though the pre-sale book itself has been shrinking ($248.0m to $239.8m in the last six months)

Ayrburn, Cracker Bay and Northbrook retirement villages are new, unproven revenue streams still in ramp-up; provide some cushion against residential cyclicality but are small relative to the balance sheet capital committed
Sunfield and Ayrburn Screen Hub both accepted into the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 process, giving a faster consenting pathway than standard RMA processes - though this has proven contentious

weaknesses: High project concentration - a small number of large developments (Sunfield, Northlake, Lakeside, Ayrburn, Northbrook) drive most value, so single-project execution or legal risk is material
No brand-based pricing power; residential settlements are price-takers in a soft NZ housing market
Governance and key-person risk crystallized in 2026 with founder/CEO departure and a near-complete board walkout
Balance sheet increasingly encumbered - secured borrowings rose from zero (FY22) to ~$119m (H1 FY26) against specific projects (Cracker Bay, Northlake Stage 18, Sunfield, Lakeside)

growth_drivers: c.5,750-unit landbank pipeline across 20 masterplanned communities provides multi-year runway once market conditions improve
Sunfield (Auckland, targeting ~4,000+ residents) fast-track approval, if it survives legal challenge, would unlock a major new revenue source

Ramp-up of recurring-income assets: Northbrook Wānaka retirement village (Stage Two/Welcome Building and Premium Care Suites under construction), Cracker Bay office leasing (77% leased as at Dec-25), and Ayrburn hospitality precinct (over a million visitors/year target)
Ayrburn Screen Hub (film studio + accommodation) awaiting a fast-track decision, expected to add incremental hospitality revenue
South Island focus (Queenstown-Lakes District) where management says the market has remained comparatively buoyant versus Auckland
Eventual NZ interest-rate easing cycle and housing market recovery would re-accelerate settlement volumes and margins from currently depressed levels
Cracker Bay Hospitality precinct (first restaurant Bravo opened Feb 2026) adds further diversification

business.description: Units settled have fallen from 565 (FY23) to 266 (FY25) to just 14 in H1 FY26, an almost complete stall in residential sales in the reporting company's largest segment
A large share of NAV and future earnings sits in a handful of projects (Sunfield, Northlake, Lakeside, Ayrburn, Northbrook); a setback at any one is highly consequential

Chris Meehan resigned as CEO/Chair in July 2026 amid an internal investigation and multiple staff misconduct complaints (including harassment allegations); this triggered a board exodus in August 2026 (Chair Steven Joyce, director Guy Fergusson, executive director Julian Cook) citing 'fundamental misalignment' with majority shareholder Meehan over governance, leaving the board briefly non-compliant with NZX independence rules and triggering a trading suspension (31 Aug-3 Sep 2026)
Meehan retains ~55% ownership and a board seat and consulting role on major projects despite stepping down as CEO/Chair, creating an overhang of influence and potential further governance friction

Auckland Council is challenging the Sunfield fast-track approval in the High Court alleging legal errors by the panel; Kāinga Ora is reportedly suing Winton for ~$138m over an alleged failure to fast-track the development; both could delay or impair Winton's largest single project

financial.description: NPAT fell from $64.6m (FY23) to $15.8m (FY24) to $10.3m (FY25), with a small loss in H1 FY25 (-$2.0m) and H1 FY26 (-$0.9m); FY25 NPAT margin only 6.6%
Borrowings grew from $0 (FY22) to $99.4m (FY25) to $119.4m (H1 FY26), secured against Cracker Bay, Northlake Stage 18, Sunfield and Lakeside; cash fell to $14.5m by Dec-25 from $41.7m a year earlier
Board paused dividends from FY25 onward 'to maintain financial discipline through softer market conditions'
Large inventory and investment-property balances ($225.7m and $358.4m respectively at FY25) tie up capital that generates no return until settlement or lease-up

regulatory.description: Reliance on the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 for Sunfield and Ayrburn Screen Hub is now under direct legal challenge (Auckland Council High Court case), creating precedent risk for the whole fast-track pathway Winton depends on for growth
Sunfield is sited partly on a flood plain and highly productive rural land, drawing infrastructure and environmental objections from Auckland Council
The August 2026 board resignations breached minimum independent-director requirements, resulting in a real (if brief) trading suspension - a recurrence risk if governance remains unsettled

macro.description: Building consents, ready-mix concrete volumes (33.8% below Dec-21 peak) and net migration are all depressed; unemployment rose to 5.4% by Dec-25, the highest since 2016-17, and management explicitly does not expect a substantial housing recovery until unemployment peaks
Falling OCR is a modest tailwind but buyer affordability and Winton's own project-debt servicing costs remain sensitive to the rate path
Cordell Construction Cost Index remains elevated versus history even as volumes fall, compressing margins on built product
Auckland market (where Sunfield sits) described as particularly subdued, while Queenstown-Lakes has outperformed - an uneven recovery could leave Winton's largest project lagging

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ residential development remains in a cyclical downturn - building consents, ready-mix concrete volumes and net migration all below long-run averages as of late 2025/H1 2026, with unemployment still rising (5.4% Dec-25, highest since 2016-17). Management does not expect a substantial turnaround until unemployment peaks, though a declining OCR and improved house sales in some regions (notably Queenstown-Lakes) are early positive signals.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - core land/section settlement revenue is directly tied to the NZ housing cycle, buyer confidence, credit availability and employment; recurring-income diversification (retirement, commercial, hospitality) is still small relative to the cyclical core
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - both for buyer affordability/mortgage serviceability (demand side) and for Winton's own project-level secured borrowings (cost side); an easing OCR is a genuine but gradual tailwind
key_input_costs: Construction/materials costs (Cordell Construction Cost Index elevated)
Labour costs (noted as easing per FY25 commentary)

recent_developments.event: Founder Chris Meehan resigned as CEO and Chair 'during the concluding stages of a Board-led employment process' following an internal investigation into workplace conduct complaints; remains a director and project consultant. Steven Joyce (independent director) elected interim Chair; Julian Cook took an expanded interim executive role.

Chair Steven Joyce and director Guy Fergusson resigned effective 31 Aug, followed by executive director Julian Cook and committee-chair James Kemp (Kemp remained a director), all citing 'fundamental misalignment' with majority shareholder Meehan over board independence and governance standards

NZ RegCo suspended quotation of Winton shares on both NZX and ASX after the board fell below minimum independent-director requirements; trading resumed 3 Sept 2026 after Michael Stiassny was appointed independent Chair and board committees were reconstituted for compliance
FY25 results reported to market: revenue $155.4m (down 10.5% YoY), NPAT $10.3m, 266 units settled (vs 345 FY24); dividend remained paused

Full-year results showed a rebound: revenue $188.8m (+21.5% YoY), EBITDA $45.6m (+114%), NPAT $22.7m (+120% YoY) on 430 units settled, even as shares fell ~6.8% on results day amid governance overhang
H1 FY26 revenue collapsed to $32.4m (down 60% YoY) on only 14 units settled (vs 90 in H1 FY25); small net loss of $0.9m; pre-sale book $239.8m; commercial/Ayrburn revenue grew
Fast-track Expert Panel issued draft decision approving the Sunfield masterplanned community

Auckland Council commenced High Court legal challenge against the Sunfield fast-track approval alleging panel legal errors (flood-plain/rural land and infrastructure concerns); Kāinga Ora reported separately pursuing Winton for ~$138m related to fast-track process disputes
Reports that Winton's top in-house lawyer resigned as the company heads into the pivotal Auckland Council court case over Sunfield

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2026 Interim Results (20 February 2026) and FY2026 Annual Results (~August 2026)

items.notes: Board suspended dividends 'to maintain financial discipline through softer market conditions' while still funding growth capex; no resumption date given as of H1 FY26

items.target: Northlake Stage 18 and Lakeside debt expected to be repaid in full from H2 FY26 settlements
items.notes: Management flagged debt profile 'set to reduce' as specific project facilities are repaid from forecast settlements

items.target: No substantial recovery expected until unemployment peaks
items.notes: Qualitative guidance only, reiterated across FY25 annual and H1 FY26 interim commentary; management says it is being 'judicious' about committing further capital until there is conviction the market has turned

items.target: Prioritise Sunfield and South Island (Queenstown-Lakes) projects
items.notes: Management explicitly narrowing focus to where market conditions are comparatively resilient, deferring capital elsewhere (e.g., Cracker Bay/Wynyard Quarter construction timing pending market improvement)

guidance.management_commentary: As of the FY25 annual result and H1 FY26 interim, management (then CEO Chris Meehan/CFO Jean McMahon) described a 'continued difficult property market and very challenging economic conditions,' citing record-low net migration, elevated unemployment, and subdued building consents, while noting early positive signs (falling OCR, more house sales, easing labour costs, especially in Queenstown-Lakes). No formal quantitative revenue/earnings guidance range for FY26/FY27 was identified in the extracted materials; subsequent FY26 full-year results (reported publicly, not in the extracted filings) showed revenue of $188.8m and NPAT of $22.7m, indicating a partial recovery in settlement volumes to 430 units for the year, even as the governance crisis unfolded around the same reporting period.

bull_case: Large, largely-consented landbank (c.5,750 units across 20 projects) gives multi-year optionality once the housing cycle turns, without needing to re-source land

FY2026 full-year results (revenue +21.5% to $188.8m, NPAT +120% to $22.7m, 430 units settled) suggest the worst of the settlement collapse may be behind the company, even before a full market recovery

Diversification into recurring-income assets (Ayrburn hospitality, Cracker Bay office leasing, Northbrook retirement village) is beginning to reduce reliance on lumpy residential settlements and is scaling (Cracker Bay 77% leased, Ayrburn approaching 1m annual visitors)

Governance reset with independent, well-regarded new Chair Michael Stiassny and reconstituted board committees may restore market confidence and reduce founder-control risk after the August 2026 crisis

Share price has fallen dramatically from IPO ($1.15bn valuation, $3.87/share) to roughly $1 and a ~$300-400m market cap, alongside analyst consensus price targets in the NZ$2.40-2.80 range, implying meaningful upside if execution and governance stabilize

Falling OCR and stronger regional (Queenstown-Lakes) housing activity are incremental tailwinds; NTA per share has been broadly stable/rising ($178.7c as at Dec-25) despite the earnings downturn, suggesting asset backing has not eroded
bear_case: Core residential settlement volumes have essentially collapsed (14 units in H1 FY26 vs 553 in FY18), and management itself says no substantial recovery is likely until unemployment peaks - timing entirely outside the company's control

Governance crisis is unresolved at a structural level: majority shareholder Meehan (~55%) retains board influence and a consulting role despite the conduct allegations that triggered his exit, and the August 2026 mass resignation shows continuing friction between the board and controlling shareholder

Sunfield, the flagship growth project, faces a High Court challenge from Auckland Council and a reported ~$138m claim from Kāinga Ora; an adverse outcome would remove the single largest identified growth driver and could trigger further legal/reputational costs

Rising secured debt ($119.4m by Dec-25, up from zero in FY22) against a backdrop of falling cash ($14.5m) and paused dividends signals tightening financial flexibility in a market that has not yet turned

Reputational overhang from widely reported harassment allegations against the founder, political-donation scrutiny, and ongoing litigation could deter both institutional investors and prospective JV/capital partners, compounding the earnings downturn
